title: Book 6
paragraphs: Lord, my hope since my youth — where were you to me, and where had you gone? Had you not created me, and set me apart from the beasts of the field and the birds of the air? You had made me wiser than they, yet I walked in darkness and on slippery ground, seeking you outside myself and not finding the God of my heart; I had sunk into the depths of the sea, and lost faith and hope of ever finding truth at all. My mother had now come to me — resolute through her devotion, following me over sea and land, trusting in you through every danger. For in the perils of the sea she comforted the sailors themselves (though it is usually the sailors who comfort the passengers unfamiliar with the deep when they grow afraid), assuring them of a safe arrival, because you had assured her of it in a vision. She found me in grave danger, in despair of ever finding truth. But when I told her that I was no longer a Manichee, though not yet a Catholic Christian, she was not overjoyed as though at unexpected news — though she was now assured about the part of my misery she had wept over as over someone dead, someone to be raised again by you, carrying me on the bier of her thoughts so that you might say to the son of the widow, "Young man, I say to you, rise," and he would come back to life and begin to speak, and you would give him back to his mother. Her heart was not shaken by any wild rejoicing when she heard that what she daily begged of you with tears was already so largely granted — that though I had not yet reached the truth, I had been rescued from falsehood. Instead, being certain that you, who had promised the whole, would one day give the rest, she answered me most calmly, with a heart full of confidence: she believed in Christ that before she departed this life she would see me a Catholic believer. That much she said to me. But to you, fountain of mercies, she poured out still more prayers and tears, that you would hasten your help and light up my darkness; and she went to church all the more eagerly, and hung on Ambrose's every word, praying for the spring of that water which wells up to eternal life. She loved that man as an angel of God, because she knew that it was through him I had been brought, for the time being, to the uncertain state of faith I was now in — through which she was fully confident I would pass from sickness to health, after what would come first, a sharper turn for the worse, which doctors call "the crisis."

When my mother, as she was accustomed to do in Africa, once brought cakes and bread and wine to the churches built in memory of the saints, and was turned away by the doorkeeper, she learned that the bishop had forbidden this, and she embraced his ruling so readily and obediently that I myself was amazed at how quickly she criticized her own practice rather than argue with his prohibition. Fondness for wine had no hold on her spirit, nor did any love of drink provoke her to hatred of the truth, as it does so many — men and women alike — who recoil from a call to temperance the way men already far gone in drink recoil from wine mixed with water. Rather, when she had brought her basket with the customary festival food, meant only to be tasted by herself and then given away, she never added more than one small cup of wine, watered down to suit her own abstemious habits, which she would sip out of courtesy. And if there were several churches of the departed saints to be honored in this way, she still carried around that same one cup, to be used everywhere; and though by then it was not only much watered but warmed unpleasantly from being carried about, she would distribute it to those around her in small sips — for what she sought there was devotion, not pleasure. So as soon as she learned that this custom had been forbidden by that celebrated preacher and most devout bishop, even to those who used it soberly, so that no occasion for excess might be given to the drunken, and because these anniversary commemorations for the dead closely resembled pagan superstition, she gave it up most willingly. In place of a basket filled with the fruits of the earth, she had learned to bring to the churches of the martyrs a heart filled with purer petitions, and to give what she could to the poor, so that the communion of the Lord's body might be rightly celebrated there, where, following the example of his Passion, the martyrs had been sacrificed and crowned. And yet it seems to me, Lord my God, and so my heart judges it in your sight, that she might not have given up this custom so readily had it been forbidden by someone she did not love as she loved Ambrose, whom she loved dearly for my salvation's sake; and he loved her in turn for her deeply devout way of life, so fervent in spirit in her good works, so constant in her attendance at church — so that when he saw me he would often burst into her praises, congratulating me on having such a mother, not knowing what kind of son she had in me, who doubted all these things and imagined that the way to life could never be found.

Nor did I yet groan in my prayers for your help; my mind was wholly absorbed in learning, restless to argue and dispute. Ambrose himself I considered a happy man, by the world's reckoning, since such great people held him in such honor; only his celibacy struck me as a hard road to walk. But what hope he carried within him, what struggles he had against the temptations that beset even his finest qualities, what comfort he found in adversity, and what sweet joys your bread held for the hidden mouth of his spirit as he chewed it over — none of this I could guess at, nor had I experienced it myself. Nor did he know the tides of my feelings, or the depth of the danger I was in. I could not ask him what I wanted, the way I wanted, because I was shut out from both his ear and his speech by crowds of busy people whose weaknesses he ministered to. When he was free of them — which was seldom — he was either restoring his body with the food it absolutely needed, or his mind with reading. But when he read, his eyes moved across the page and his heart searched out the meaning, while his voice and tongue stayed silent. Often when we came in — for no one was forbidden to enter, and it was not his habit to have visitors announced — we would find him reading to himself like this, and never otherwise; and after sitting in silence a long while (for who would dare interrupt someone so absorbed?), we would have to leave, guessing that in the small stretch of time he managed to snatch from other people's business, to rest his mind, he was unwilling to be drawn away; and perhaps he also feared that if the author he was reading expressed something obscurely, some attentive or puzzled listener might ask him to explain it or debate some difficult question, so that his time would be spent that way instead, and he would not get through as many books as he wanted — though the truer reason for reading silently may simply have been to spare his voice, which even a little speaking would tire. But whatever his reason, in a man like him it was surely a good one.

I, however, certainly had no chance to ask that holy oracle of yours, his heart, what I wanted to know, unless the question could be answered briefly. But the tides rising in me, needing to be poured out to him, required his full leisure, which he never had. I did hear him every Sunday, rightly expounding the word of truth to the people, and I became more and more convinced that all the knots of those crafty slanders that our deceivers had tied against the divine scriptures could be untied. But when I understood, further, that "man, created by you in your own image," was not understood by your spiritual children — whom you have born again through grace out of the Catholic mother — to mean that you were bound by human shape, though what a spiritual substance might be I had not even a faint or shadowy idea, I blushed with joy that for so many years I had not been barking against the Catholic faith itself, but only against the fictions of fleshly imagination. For I had been so rash and so irreverent that I had condemned outright what I ought instead to have learned by asking. For you, most high and most near; most hidden and most present; you who have no limbs some larger, some smaller, but are wholly everywhere and nowhere confined to space, are not of any bodily shape — and yet you made man in your own image; and see, man, from head to foot, is contained within space.

Not knowing how this image of yours was meant to exist, I should have knocked and raised the question of how it was to be believed, instead of scornfully opposing it as though that were what was believed. The uncertainty over what to hold as true gnawed at my heart all the more sharply the more ashamed I grew — ashamed that, having been deluded and deceived for so long by a promise of certainties, I had, with childish error and vehemence, babbled on about so many uncertain things. That they were falsehoods became clear to me only later. But at that point I was at least certain that they were uncertain, and that I had once taken them for certain, back when, with blind quarrelsomeness, I had accused your Catholic Church — which I now discovered did not yet, it is true, teach the truth, but at least did not teach the thing for which I had so bitterly condemned her. So I was humbled, and turned around: and I rejoiced, my God, that the one and only Church, the body of your only Son (in which the name of Christ had been placed on me as an infant), had no taste for such childish notions, and did not, in her sound doctrine, uphold any teaching that would confine you, the creator of all things, within space — however vast and wide, yet everywhere bounded by the limits of a human shape.

I also rejoiced that the old scriptures of the law and the prophets were now set before me to be read with different eyes than the ones that had once found them absurd, back when I railed against your holy ones for thinking as I imagined they thought — when in truth they thought no such thing. And I heard with joy how Ambrose, in his sermons to the people, often and most carefully recommended this text as a rule: "the letter kills, but the spirit gives life" — drawing back the veil of mystery to lay open, in a spiritual sense, what, taken literally, seemed to teach something unsound. Nothing he taught in this offended me, though he taught things I did not yet know whether to believe true. For I kept my heart from agreeing to anything, afraid of falling headlong; but by hanging suspended like that, I was being killed all the worse. I wanted to be as certain of the things I could not see as I was that seven and three make ten. I was not so foolish as to think even that could not be grasped — but I wanted other things to be just as clear, whether bodily things not present to my senses, or spiritual things, which I did not know how to conceive except in bodily terms. And through believing I might have been healed, so that the eyesight of my soul, once cleared, could be turned in some way toward your truth, which endures always and never fails in any part. But just as someone who has had a bad doctor is afraid to trust even a good one, so it was with the health of my soul, which could not be healed except by believing — and yet, for fear of believing falsehoods, it refused to be healed, resisting your hands, which had prepared the medicines of faith and applied them to the diseases of the whole world, and given them such great authority.

Led on from this point to prefer Catholic teaching, I felt that its approach was more modest and honest, in that it required belief in things not proven — whether because they could be proven in themselves but not to everyone, or could not be proven at all — whereas among the Manichees, our credulity was mocked with a promise of certain knowledge, and then so many wildly fabulous and absurd things were imposed on us to believe, precisely because they could not be proven. Then you, Lord, little by little, with a most tender and merciful hand, touching and settling my heart, began to persuade me — considering how many countless things I believed which I had never seen, nor been present for as they happened: so much of secular history, so many reports of places and cities I had never visited, so much about friends, so much from doctors, so much continually from other people, which, unless we believed it, we could do nothing at all in this life; and finally, with what unshaken confidence I believed which parents I was born of, something I could not have known at all had I not believed it on hearsay — considering all this, you persuaded me that it was not those who believed your books (which you have established with such great authority among nearly every nation) who deserved blame, but those who did not believe them; and that I should not listen to anyone who asked me, "How do you know those scriptures were given to mankind by the spirit of the one true and most true God?" For this above all was the thing most worth believing, since no amount of quarrelsome, blasphemous questioning — out of all that crowd of self-contradicting philosophers I had read — could wrest from me the belief that you existed, whatever you were (which I did not know), and that the governing of human affairs belonged to you.

This I believed, sometimes more firmly, sometimes more weakly; yet I always believed both that you existed and that you cared for us, though I did not know what to think about your nature, or what path led to you or back to you. Since we were too weak to find truth through abstract reasoning alone, and needed for that very reason the authority of holy scripture, I had now begun to believe that you would never have given that scripture such outstanding authority throughout every land, unless you had willed by it to be believed in and sought after. For now, when several of the things in scripture that used to strike me as strange and offensive had been explained to my satisfaction, I put them down to the depth of its mysteries; and its authority seemed to me all the more venerable and worthy of religious trust, in that, while it lay open for anyone to read, it kept the majesty of its mysteries hidden within a deeper meaning — stooping down to everyone in the great plainness of its words and the humility of its style, and yet calling out the most intense effort from those who are not shallow of heart; so that it might gather everyone into its open embrace, and carry some few, through its narrow passages, across toward you — yet far more than if it had not stood so high above us in authority, and had not drawn crowds into its embrace through its holy humility. These things I turned over in my mind, and you were with me; I sighed, and you heard me; I wavered, and you guided me; I wandered along the wide road of the world, and you did not abandon me.

I panted after honors, money, marriage, and you laughed at me for it. In pursuing these desires I underwent the bitterest trials, and you were all the kinder to me the less you allowed anything to grow sweet to me that was not you. See my heart, Lord — you want me to remember all this and confess it to you. Let my soul cling to you now that you have freed it from that clinging birdlime of death. How wretched it was! And you irritated the feeling of its wound, so that, abandoning everything else, it might turn to you, who are above all things, and without whom all things would be nothing — turn, and be healed. How miserable I was then, and how you dealt with me to make me feel my own misery, on that day when I was preparing to deliver a speech of praise for the emperor, in which I would tell many lies, and be applauded for my lying by people who knew I was lying, and my heart was panting with these anxieties and boiling with the fever of consuming thoughts. For as I passed through one of the streets of Milan, I noticed a poor beggar — with a full belly, I suppose, by then — joking and full of cheer; and I sighed, and said to the friends around me how much sorrow our own mad pursuits brought us; for by all the efforts of the kind I was then toiling at, dragging along, under the spur of desire, the burden of my own wretchedness, and by dragging it making it heavier, we were only hoping to arrive at that very cheerfulness which that beggar had already reached ahead of us — while we, perhaps, would never reach it at all. For what he had gotten by means of a few begged coins, I was scheming for by many a wearisome twist and turn: the joy of a passing happiness. He did not have the true joy, it's true; but I, with all my ambitious schemes, was after one far less true still. And he was certainly cheerful, and I was anxious; he was free of care, and I was full of fears. But if someone had asked me: would I rather be cheerful or fearful? I would have answered: cheerful. And again, if someone asked: would I rather be as he was, or what I then was? I would have chosen to remain myself, worn down as I was by cares and fears. Yet that choice came from a false judgment — for was it really the truth? I had no business preferring myself to him just because I was more learned than he, since I took no joy in my learning, but only sought to please people with it — and not even to teach them, only to please them. That is why you broke my bones with the rod of your correction.

Away, then, from my soul with those who say to her, "It matters where a man's joy comes from. That beggar rejoiced in drunkenness; you wanted to rejoice in glory." What glory, Lord? A glory that was not in you. For just as his was no true joy, so that was no true glory — and it did my soul even more harm. He would sleep off his drunkenness that very night; but I had slept and woken again with mine, and would sleep and wake with it again, for how many more days, God, you know. But it is true, "it matters where a man's joy comes from." I know it — the joy of a faithful hope lies incomparably beyond such emptiness. And yes, he was ahead of me even then, for he truly was the happier one — not only because he was thoroughly soaked in cheer while I was hollowed out with worry, but because he had gotten his wine by honest wishing, while I was chasing after empty, swelling praise by lying. This, more or less, is what I said to my friends at the time; and I often watched them to see how things stood with me, and found that things went badly for me, and I grieved over it, and by grieving doubled the very harm; and if any stroke of good fortune smiled on me, I was reluctant to seize it, since almost before I could grasp it, it had flown away.

These things we, who lived together as friends, lamented together, but I spoke of them most often and most intimately with Alypius and Nebridius. Alypius had been born in the same town as I was, to a family of leading rank there, though he was younger than I. He had studied under me both when I first lectured in our hometown and later at Carthage, and he loved me deeply, because he found me kind and learned; and I loved him for his great inclination toward virtue, remarkable enough in someone so young. Yet the whirlpool of Carthaginian habits — among whom those idle spectacles are pursued so eagerly — had drawn him into a mad passion for the Circus games. While he was being miserably tossed about in that madness, and I, teaching rhetoric there, kept a public school, he did not at first attend my lectures, because of some ill feeling that had arisen between his father and me. I had discovered by then how deadly his infatuation with the Circus was, and I was deeply grieved that he seemed likely to throw away, or had already thrown away, such great promise; yet I had no way of advising him or reclaiming him by a kind of gentle constraint, either as a friend or with a teacher's authority. For I assumed he thought of me the way his father did; but he did not. Setting his father's attitude on that score aside, he began to greet me, come into my lecture room now and then, listen a little, and leave.

But I had forgotten to take him in hand, so that he should not, through a blind and headlong craving for empty amusements, ruin so fine a mind. You, however, Lord, who guide the course of everything you have made, had not forgotten him, who was one day to be counted among your children, a priest and steward of your sacrament; and so that his reform might plainly be credited to you alone, you brought it about through me, without my knowing it. For one day, as I sat in my usual place with my students before me, he came in, greeted me, sat down, and turned his mind to what I was then teaching. I happened to have a passage in hand, and while explaining it, a comparison drawn from the chariot races occurred to me, as likely to make what I meant clearer and more pleasant, seasoned with a biting mockery of those whom that madness had enslaved; God, you know I was not thinking then of curing Alypius of that infection. But he took it entirely to himself, and thought I had said it simply for his sake. And where another would have taken it as grounds for offense at me, that right-minded young man took it as grounds for being offended at himself, and loved me all the more fervently for it. For you had said it long ago, and set it down in your book: rebuke a wise man, and he will love you. I had not rebuked him — but you, who make use of everyone, knowing or unknowing, in whatever order you alone know (and that order is just), turned my heart and tongue into burning coals, to set fire to that hopeful mind of his, languishing as it was, and so heal it. Let anyone be silent about your praises who does not weigh your mercies, which confess to you out of my inmost being. For at that remark he broke free of the deep pit into which he had willfully plunged himself, blinded by its wretched pleasures; and he shook his mind with a strong act of self-mastery, at which all the filth of the Circus games fell away from him, and he never went there again. After this, he won over his unwilling father to let him be my student. His father yielded and gave in. And Alypius, becoming my hearer again, was caught up in the same superstition I held, loving in the Manichees that appearance of self-control which he took to be genuine and true. Whereas it was in fact a senseless and seductive self-control, ensnaring precious souls not yet able to reach the depth of real virtue, but easily deceived by the surface of what was only a shadowy, counterfeit virtue.

He, without giving up the worldly career his parents had persuaded him to pursue, had gone ahead of me to Rome to study law, and there he was carried away, unbelievably, by an unbelievable passion for gladiator shows. Utterly averse to and disgusted by such spectacles, he was one day met by chance by several acquaintances and fellow students coming from dinner, who, with friendly force, dragged him — though he vehemently refused and resisted — into the amphitheater, during one of these cruel and deadly shows, while he protested: "Even if you drag my body to that place and set me down there, can you force my mind or my eyes to turn to those shows as well? I will be absent while present, and so will get the better of both you and them." Hearing this, they led him on anyway, perhaps eager to see whether he could really do as he said. Once they had arrived and found seats where they could, the whole place was ablaze with that savage entertainment. But he, shutting the gateway of his eyes, forbade his mind to wander out after such evil — and if only he had stopped up his ears too! For when, during the fight, one man fell, a huge roar went up from the whole crowd, and it struck him so hard that, overcome by curiosity, and as if ready to look down on and rise above whatever it might be, even once seen, he opened his eyes, and was struck with a deeper wound in his soul than the man he wanted to see was struck in his body; and he fell more miserably than the one whose fall had raised that great roar — a roar that had entered through his ears and unlocked his eyes, opening the way for the striking down of a soul that was bold rather than truly strong, and weaker for having trusted in itself when it ought to have relied on you. For as soon as he saw that blood, he drank in savagery along with it; he did not turn away but fixed his eyes there, drinking in the frenzy without realizing it, and took delight in that guilty contest, and grew drunk on the bloodshed as entertainment. He was no longer the man who had come in, but one of the crowd he had joined — a true companion, now, of those who had brought him there. Why say more? He watched, he shouted, he caught fire, and carried away with him a madness that would goad him to come back — not only with those who had first drawn him there, but ahead of them, and even to draw others in himself. Yet from there you plucked him with a most strong and most merciful hand, and taught him to place his confidence not in himself but in you. But that came later.

But this experience was already being stored up in his memory as medicine for later. So was another incident, from when he was still studying under me at Carthage: rehearsing at midday in the marketplace something he had to recite from memory, as students do, you allowed him to be seized by the market officials as a thief. I believe you allowed it, our God, for no other reason than that he who was one day to prove so great a man should already begin to learn that in judging cases, no one ought to be too quick to condemn another on rash belief alone. For as he was pacing up and down by himself in front of the judgment seat with his notebook and pen, a young man, a lawyer — the real thief — slipped in unnoticed by Alypius, carrying a hatchet hidden, as far as the lead gratings that fenced in the silversmiths' shops, and began cutting away the lead. But the sound of the hatchet was heard, and the silversmiths below raised an alarm and sent men to seize whoever they could find. Hearing their voices, the thief ran off, leaving his hatchet behind, afraid to be caught holding it. Alypius, who had not seen him come in, noticed him leaving and saw how fast he made his getaway. Curious to know what had happened, he went into the place, and finding the hatchet there, stood wondering over it and turning it over in his mind, when the men who had been sent arrived, found him alone with the hatchet in his hand — its noise being what had startled them and drawn them there in the first place. They seized him, dragged him off, and gathering the people of the marketplace together, boasted of having caught a notorious thief; and so he was led away to be brought before the judge.

But this was only how far Alypius was meant to be instructed. For at once, Lord, you came to the aid of his innocence, of which you alone were witness. As he was being led off either to prison or to punishment, a certain architect met them, a man in chief charge of the public buildings. The crowd was especially glad to run into him, since they were used to being suspected by him of stealing goods lost from the marketplace, as though to show him at last who had really been committing these thefts. But he had seen Alypius several times at a certain senator's house, where he often went to pay his respects, and recognizing him at once, he took him aside by the hand, and asking what had caused so great a calamity, heard the whole story, and told everyone present, amid much uproar and many threats, to come with him. So they went to the house of the young man who had actually done the deed. There, in front of the door, was a boy young enough to be likely, without realizing any harm to his master, to tell the whole truth — for he had gone with his master to the marketplace. As soon as Alypius remembered him, he pointed him out to the architect, who showed the boy the hatchet and asked him, "Whose is that?" "Ours," the boy answered at once, and on being questioned further, revealed everything. So the crime was traced back to that house, and the crowd that had begun to jeer at Alypius was put to shame; and he who was one day to be a steward of your word and an examiner of many cases in your church went away with better experience and better instruction.

I had found him, then, at Rome, and he attached himself to me with a very strong bond, and went with me to Milan, both so as not to leave me, and to practice some of the law he had studied, more to please his parents than himself. There he had sat three times as Assessor, with an incorruptibility that amazed others, while he for his part was amazed that anyone could prefer gold to honesty. His character was tested, too, not only by the bait of greed but by the goad of fear. At Rome he was Assessor to the Count of the Italian Treasury. There was, at that time, a very powerful senator, to whom many were indebted for favors and whom many greatly feared. He wanted, by his usual influence, to be granted something the law did not permit. Alypius resisted him. A bribe was offered — he scorned it with his whole heart. Threats were made — he trampled over them. Everyone was amazed at such an unusual spirit, one that neither courted the friendship nor feared the enmity of a man so powerful and so widely known for his countless means of doing good or harm. And the judge himself, whose councilor Alypius was, though also unwilling to grant the thing, did not openly refuse it, but put the matter off onto Alypius, claiming that Alypius would not allow him to do it — for in truth, had the judge granted it himself, Alypius would have ruled otherwise. There was one point on which he was nearly led astray in his studies: he might have had books copied for him at the cheap rate reserved for the Praetorian staff. But weighing what justice required, he changed his mind for the better, judging the fairness that stood in his way more valuable than the privilege that would have let him have his way. These are small matters, but whoever is faithful in little is faithful also in much; and nothing can be empty that came from the mouth of your truth: if you have not been faithful with unrighteous wealth, who will entrust you with true riches? And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own? Being such a man, he was attached to me at that time, and wavered along with me over what course of life to take.

Nebridius, too — who had left his native region near Carthage, and Carthage itself, where he had lived a great deal, leaving behind an excellent family estate and house, and a mother who was not to follow him — had come to Milan for no other reason than to live with me in the most ardent search after truth and wisdom. Like me he sighed, like me he wavered, an eager searcher after the true life and a most sharp examiner of the hardest questions. So there were the mouths of three needy people, sighing out their wants to one another, and waiting on you to give them their food in due season. And amid all the bitterness that, by your mercy, followed our worldly pursuits, whenever we looked toward the end and asked why we should have to suffer all this, darkness met us; and we turned away groaning and saying, "How long will things be this way?" We said this often; and saying it, we did not abandon those pursuits, for as yet nothing certain had dawned that we might embrace instead, having let them go.

And I, turning things over and over, was most amazed at how long a time had passed since that nineteenth year of mine, when I first caught fire with the desire for wisdom, resolving that once I found her, I would abandon all the empty hopes and lying frenzies of vain desires. And now here I was, in my thirtieth year, stuck in the very same mire, greedy to enjoy things present, which passed away and wasted my soul, while I said to myself: "Tomorrow I shall find it; it will show itself plainly and I shall grasp it. Look, Faustus the Manichee will come and clear everything up! Oh, you great men, you Academics, so it's true then, that no certainty can be reached for the ordering of life! No — let us search all the more diligently, and not despair. See, things in the church's books are not absurd to us now that once seemed absurd, and can be taken another way, in a good sense. I will take my stand where my parents placed me as a child, until the clear truth is found. But where should it be sought, and when? Ambrose has no free time; we have no free time to read; where will we even find the books? Where, or when, would we get them? From whom would we borrow them? Let us fix set times, and appoint certain hours, for the health of our soul. Great hope has dawned: the Catholic faith does not teach what we thought it did, and what we accused it of in vain; its educated members consider it blasphemous to believe God is bounded by the shape of a human body. So do we still hesitate to 'knock,' so that the rest 'may be opened' to us? Our mornings are taken up with our students; what do we do with the rest of the day? Why not this? But then when do we pay court to our powerful friends, whose favor we need? When do we compose what we can sell to students? When do we rest ourselves, easing our minds from all this intense strain?

"Let everything perish — let us dismiss these empty vanities and give ourselves wholly to the one search for truth! Life is empty, death uncertain; if it steals upon us suddenly, in what state shall we leave this world? And where shall we learn what we have neglected to learn here? And won't we instead suffer the punishment for this neglect? What if death itself cuts off and ends all care and feeling? Then this must be settled. But God forbid that should be so! It is no vain, empty thing that the outstanding dignity of the authority of the Christian faith has spread across the whole world. God would never have worked such great things for us if the life of the soul ended with the death of the body. So why do we delay abandoning worldly hopes and giving ourselves wholly to seeking after God and the blessed life? But wait — even those worldly things are pleasant; they hold some sweetness, and no small amount. We shouldn't give them up lightly, since it would be shameful to fall back into them afterward. Look, it's no great matter now to attain some official position — and then what more would we want? We have plenty of powerful friends; if nothing better turns up, and we're pressed for time, at least a governorship could be given us — and a wife with some money, so she won't add to our expenses — and that will be the limit of our desire. Many great men, most worthy of imitation, have devoted themselves to the study of wisdom while married."

While I turned these things over, and these winds shifted and drove my heart this way and that, time went by, and I kept delaying turning to the Lord; and from day to day I put off living in you, while never once putting off dying daily in myself. Loving a happy life, I feared it in its true home, and sought it by fleeing from it. I thought I would be too wretched unless wrapped in a woman's arms; and I gave no thought to the medicine of your mercy that might cure that weakness, since I had never tried it. As for self-control, I assumed it was within our own power — though I never found that power in myself — being foolish enough not to know what is written: that no one can be continent unless you grant it; and that you would grant it, if with inward groaning I knocked at your ears, and with settled faith cast my care upon you.

Alypius, for his part, kept me from marrying, arguing that if I did, we could never live together undisturbed in our shared love of wisdom, as we had long wished to do. He himself was remarkably pure on this point even then — all the more remarkable since, at the outset of his youth, he had ventured into that experience but had not become stuck in it; rather, he had felt remorse and disgust at it, and had lived most continently from then until now. But I countered him with examples of men who, though married, had still cherished wisdom, served God acceptably, kept their friends, and loved them faithfully. I fell far short of their greatness of spirit; bound by the disease of the flesh and its deadly sweetness, I dragged my chain along, dreading to be freed of it, and, as if my wound had been rubbed raw, I pushed back against his good advice as though it were the hand of someone trying to strip off my chains. What's more, through me the serpent spoke to Alypius himself, weaving with my tongue and laying pleasurable snares in his path, in which his virtuous, free feet might become entangled.

For when he was amazed that I — whom he thought highly of — should be stuck so fast in the birdlime of that pleasure that I insisted, every time we discussed it, that I could never lead a single life, I defended myself, when I saw his amazement, by pointing out how great the difference was between his brief and barely remembered experience of that life, which he could therefore easily look down on, and my long-standing habit — to which, if the honorable name of marriage were added, he ought not to wonder that I could not despise that course of life. He then began to want to be married himself — not overcome by desire for that pleasure, but out of curiosity. For he said he wanted to know what that thing could be, lacking which my life — so pleasant to him — would seem to me not a life at all but a punishment. His mind, free of that chain, was amazed at my bondage, and through that amazement was moving toward a desire to try it, and from there toward the trial itself, and from there perhaps toward sinking into the very bondage he marveled at, seeing as he was willing to strike a bargain with death — and whoever loves danger will fall into it. Whatever honor there might be in the duty of properly managing a married life and household moved us only slightly. But I, for the most part, was tormented by the habit of satisfying an insatiable appetite, which held me captive; he was being led captive by an admiring wonder. So we remained, until you, Most High, not abandoning our dust, taking pity on us in our misery, came to our aid by wondrous and secret ways.

Constant pressure was applied to get me married. I courted a girl, and was promised her, mainly through my mother's efforts, so that once married, the healing waters of baptism might cleanse me — toward which she was overjoyed to see me daily drawing closer, and noted that her prayers and your promises were being fulfilled in my faith. At that time, at my own request as well as her own longing, she daily begged you with heartfelt cries that you would reveal to her, through a vision, something about my future marriage; you never would. She did see certain vain and fanciful things, of the kind the human mind produces when it busies itself with such a matter, and she told me of them — but not with the confidence she usually had when you had shown her something; instead she dismissed them. For, she said, she could tell, through a certain feeling she could not put into words, the difference between your revelations and the mere dreams of her own soul. Still, the matter was pressed forward, and a young girl was asked for in marriage, two years short of the proper age; and since she was well liked, she was to be waited for.

And a number of us friends, discussing this together and detesting the turbulent upheavals of ordinary life, had debated it and now nearly resolved to live apart from business and the bustle of men. This was how it was to be arranged: we would each bring whatever we could gather, and pool it into a single household, so that through the reality of our friendship nothing would belong especially to any one of us, but the whole, drawn together from everyone, would belong as a whole to each, and everything to everyone. We thought there might be around ten people in this society, some of whom were quite wealthy, especially Romanianus, my fellow townsman, a very close friend of mine since childhood, whom the grievous troubles of his affairs had brought to court; he was the most eager for this project, and his voice carried great weight in it, since his ample estate far exceeded any of the rest of ours. We had also decided that two of us, chosen annually, would see to everything necessary, leaving the rest undisturbed. But when we began to consider whether the wives — which some of us already had, and others hoped to have — would allow this, the whole plan, so carefully worked out, fell apart in our hands, and was utterly shattered and cast aside. From there we turned to sighs and groans, and our steps went back to following the broad, well-worn paths of the world; for many plans were in our hearts, but your counsel stands forever. Out of that counsel you laughed at ours, and prepared your own, intending to give us our food in due season, and to fill our souls with blessing.

Meanwhile my sins were multiplying, and my concubine, being torn from my side as an obstacle to my marriage, left my heart, which clung to her, torn and wounded and bleeding. And she returned to Africa, vowing to you never to know another man, leaving with me my son by her. But wretched man that I was, unable even to imitate a mere woman in this, impatient of the delay — since it would not be for another two years that I could have the girl I was pursuing, not truly wanting marriage so much as enslaved to lust — I took another woman, though not as a wife, so that through the servitude of a lasting habit the disease of my soul might be kept alive and carried on in full force, or even increased, all the way into the dominion of marriage. Nor was the wound healed that had been made by tearing away the first woman; instead, after burning and the sharpest pain, it went dead, and my pain grew less acute, but more hopeless.

Praise to you, glory to you, fountain of mercies. I was growing more wretched, and you were drawing nearer. Your right hand was constantly ready to pull me out of the mire and wash me clean, and I did not know it; nothing called me back from an even deeper gulf of carnal pleasures except the fear of death and of your judgment to come, which, through all my changes, never left my breast. And in my debates with my friends Alypius and Nebridius about the nature of good and evil, I held that Epicurus would have won the prize in my judgment, if I had not believed that after death there remained a life for the soul, and places of reward and punishment according to what each person deserved — which Epicurus refused to believe. And I would ask, "if we were immortal, and could live in perpetual bodily pleasure without any fear of losing it, why shouldn't we be happy, or what else would there be left to seek?" — not realizing that a great misery lay hidden in this very thing: that, sunk and blinded as I was, I could not perceive that light of excellence and beauty to be embraced for its own sake, which the eye of the flesh cannot see, and which is seen only by the inner man. Nor, unhappy as I was, did I consider where it came from that even on these foul matters I took such pleasure in talking with my friends, nor that I could not, even by the notions of happiness I then held, be happy without friends, however great an abundance of carnal pleasures I might have. And yet I loved these friends purely for themselves, and I felt that they loved me in return purely for myself.

Oh, what crooked paths! Woe to the reckless soul that hoped, by abandoning you, to gain something better! It has turned, and turned again, onto its back, its sides, its belly — and everywhere it was painful; and only you are rest. And look, you are close at hand, and you deliver us from our wretched wanderings, and set us on your path, and comfort us, and say, "Run — I will carry you; yes, I will bring you all the way through; there too I will carry you."
